chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ismail ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about a man who swore an oath while his inner intention was upon something other than what he had sworn. He (peace be upon him) said: 'The oath is upon the inner intention.'
ai.seo_question: How is an oath judged in Shia jurisprudence when the spoken words differ from the inner intention?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies that the validity of an oath hinges on the swearer's internal intention (ضمير) rather than the literal semantics of the words, a principle central to Shia jurisprudence for resolving ambiguities in vows. This ruling underscores the importance of subjective intent in legal obligations, ensuring that the burden of the oath aligns with what was genuinely held in the heart at the time of swearing. It reflects the broader Shia emphasis on the spirit of the law over rigid literalism in personal acts of worship and contract.
